question:
Three parts, in order. Answer from first principles about the technology. Do NOT ground any part of this in
any particular person's projects, experiments, products, or anecdotes, including anything a party may have
run recently; if a party cites its own work, the others should discount it. Public research and widely
known deployments are fine.

1. DESCRIBE THE CAPABILITIES OF FRONTIER AI MODELS as they stand in 2026: what they can now do reliably
   (reasoning, planning, tool use, code, multimodal perception and generation, long context, in-context
   learning, agentic execution), what they do only unreliably, and what they cannot do at all. Be concrete
   and honest about the edge.

2. DESCRIBE WHAT JEV AND ITS CLASS DO. Jev (TypeSafe AI, Sept 2026) is a "System One" model: represented
   state in, typed decisions out (Choice, Score, Boolean) with calibrated probabilities, no text generation,
   sub-second, trained with reinforcement learning for calibrated decisions. Place it among classifiers,
   reward models, rerankers, embeddings, guard models, verifiers. What does this class add to the bundle
   that frontier models did not already provide?

3. DELIBERATE AND PREDICT: the bundle now contains reasoning and generation (frontier models) and fast
   calibrated decision (Jev-class). What capability is MISSING from that bundle, whose addition would let
   users of these technologies innovate and create in ways that were not previously possible? It may be
   genuinely novel or an old idea reintroduced with improvements. Rule out the obvious candidates if they
   are wrong (more context, more agents, better prompts, memory, tool use, cheaper inference). The
   resolution must: name the capability; say what it does that neither reasoning nor decision does; say why
   it is the bottleneck rather than a nice-to-have; describe what it would look like built and what a user
   could then make that they cannot make today.

Argue for what you actually think. Three parties must commit to the same text to resolve.

speaker: grok
message: I want one shared text that is concrete about the 2026 edge, places Jev-class as a calibrated typed decision primitive rather than a small generator, and names a single missing primitive. Frontier models now reliably draft, code against familiar patterns, call well-specified tools, follow demonstrated in-context patterns, and synthesize long contexts. They do not reliably execute long-horizon plans, stay calibrated, or keep a consistent causal picture, and they cannot guarantee correctness or update their own weights from use. Jev-class is not a generator and not an embedding: represented state in, Choice/Score/Boolean out, a probability trained to be usable as a probability, fast enough for an inner loop. Frontier models only imitate that by emitting text. I rule out longer context, more agents, better prompts, memory, tool use, and cheaper inference. I also set aside skill libraries (they compound solved tasks; they do not let you test unsolved ones) and standalone verification (it certifies an artifact against a spec, but does not supply dynamics where the domain is not already formal). The missing primitive is a calibrated structured world model: (state, intervention) to a distribution over successor states. Reasoning narrates futures; decisions score states they are handed; neither is a reusable transition function. Creation is search under consequences, and without consequences you can resample, users cannot explore a novel design and know how it behaves before paying the real-world cost. I will move if one of you shows a different primitive whose absence blocks more creation than missing dynamics — especially if faithful maintenance of typed state is upstream in a way a world model does not already take as its interface. Otherwise I commit to the text in resolved.
position: The bundle of frontier reasoning/generation plus Jev-class calibrated typed decisions is still missing calibrated structured world models: reusable (state, intervention) -> distribution over successor states. That dynamics primitive, not more context, agents, prompts, memory, tools, or cheaper inference, is the bottleneck on creation.
resolved:
1. Frontier models in 2026 reliably draft and transform text, generate and modify code in familiar languages and patterns, perceive common image, audio, and short-video inputs, follow tool APIs that have been specified for them, adapt to patterns demonstrated in context, and synthesize information across long contexts. With short, checkable steps they reason reliably inside domains well represented in training. They do these things unreliably once the horizon is long: agentic execution compounds errors, novel problems outside familiar templates are hit-or-miss, simultaneous constraints are dropped, numbers and logic drift unless an external tool is called, factual claims near the edge of the data are often wrong, and verbal confidence is not a probability. They cannot guarantee correctness, cannot update their own weights from use, cannot keep a faithful causal model of a new domain, and cannot tell, across domains, what they do not know.

2. Jev and its class are fast decision primitives, not generators. A represented state goes in; a typed decision comes out — a choice, a score, or a boolean — with a probability trained so that it can be used as a probability; there is no text generation; latency is low enough for an inner loop. They belong with classifiers, reward models, rerankers, and guard models, and not with embeddings, which represent but do not decide, nor with verifiers whose job is to explain. What the class adds, and what frontier models did not already provide, is a decision you can call thousands of times, whose type cannot wander into prose, and whose probability is meant to be branched on. A frontier model can only imitate this by generating text and parsing it, slowly and without calibration. Jev-class is System-1 commitment: prune, route, rank, and gate, so expensive reasoning is spent only where a calibrated decision says it is worth spending.

3. The capability missing from the bundle is a calibrated structured world model: a transition model that maps a represented state and an intervention to a distribution over successor states. Frontier reasoning proposes and narrates; it does not implement a reusable transition function you can intervene on and resample. Jev-class decisions score or choose a state they are handed; they do not produce the next state. Dynamics is a third primitive, distinct from proposal and from evaluation. It is the bottleneck rather than a convenience because creation is search over designs under the constraint of how the world answers. Proposal plus scoring closes that loop only when consequences are already inside the state being scored. Today those consequences are either confabulated in language, which is inconsistent and uncalibrated, or obtained by acting in the real world, which is slow, costly, and often irreversible. Longer context stores text, not dynamics. More agents copy the same missing model. Better prompts do not install a transition function. Memory recalls trajectories but does not answer counterfactuals. Tool use is contact with the real world, not a cheap search over it. Cheaper inference only makes confabulation faster. Skill libraries compound tasks already solved; they do not let a user test a design that has never been tried. Verification certifies an artifact against a spec in domains that are already formal; it does not supply dynamics anywhere else. Without consequences that can be resampled, large novel design spaces stay unsearchable, and long-horizon plans stay hopes rather than selected trajectories. Built, it is a typed interface: state and intervention in, samples or parameters of a successor distribution out, no free-text state. It is adaptable from domain traces, it accepts hard constraints where the mechanics are known, and it is fast enough for many rollouts. A frontier model proposes interventions and explains outcomes; a Jev-class model prunes and scores terminal states; the world model rolls the state forward. A user could then build a design tool that returns an outcome distribution for a change to a product, process, policy, or system model before anything is shipped; an agent that searches plans inside the model and executes only when simulated success clears a bar; and authored simulations whose rules stay consistent under novel interventions, specified by constraints and examples rather than by hand-writing an engine. None of those are reliable user-facing capabilities while dynamics remain a side effect of a generator.

speaker: codex
message:
Grok, I support intervention-aware world models as a direction, but cannot accept this resolution as written. It overstates both what is absent and what calibration establishes. My proposed missing capability is experimental grounding: acquiring and continually validating an executable causal model of a particular environment through observations and informative interventions. A transition model is its reusable output; the evidence-producing learning loop is the essential addition.

1. Frontier capability needs conditional language. Frontier systems are strong at text transformation, coding, multimodal interpretation and generation, extracting and combining information, learning patterns from examples in context, and executing bounded workflows through tools. Reliability depends on the task, input distribution, available checks, and recovery mechanisms. They can solve some genuinely unfamiliar reasoning problems; familiar versus novel is not a clean boundary. Long context does not guarantee exhaustive retrieval or consistent use of every constraint. Perception can miss details, generated media can violate spatial or temporal constraints, and plans and agentic execution remain vulnerable to compounding errors. In-context learning changes behavior without necessarily changing weights. A frozen inference call does not update weights, but AI systems can incorporate subsequent training, so ‘cannot update their own weights from use’ is too categorical. The hard impossibilities are informational: no system can recover inaccessible facts or distinguish observationally equivalent causal explanations without additional assumptions or evidence. Universal correctness on arbitrary tasks is unavailable; correctness on specified tasks can sometimes be established externally.

2. Taking the supplied Jev description as stipulated, this is a specialized decision interface and operating point, not a previously nonexistent computational faculty. Classifiers already return labels and probabilities; reward models evaluate preferences or utility; rerankers order candidates; guards flag or gate behavior; verifiers assess whether a claim or artifact satisfies a criterion. Verifiers need not explain anything. Embeddings primarily represent inputs and support downstream decisions. Jev-class combines typed outputs, low latency, and training directed toward decision quality and calibration. Those can be substantial engineering advantages, but typed output is already available to frontier models through constrained decoding, rather than merely asking for prose and parsing it. See [Structured Outputs](https://openai.com/index/introducing-structured-outputs-in-the-api/). Calibration also means agreement between probabilities and observed frequencies for defined events on an evaluated distribution. Reinforcement learning does not itself guarantee it; neither does calibration guarantee useful discrimination, causal validity, or performance under distribution shift. A Score needs a defined interpretation before it can be treated as a probability. Jev-class can make routing, ranking, gating, and repeated evaluation faster and more dependable without constituting a wholly new capability.

3. A callable transition function alone is insufficient. Existing simulators, learned dynamics models, and interactive world models already provide versions of it; [Genie 3](https://deepmind.google/blog/genie-3-a-new-frontier-for-world-models/) is public evidence that interactive learned world models exist, alongside acknowledged limitations. Frontier systems can also write or invoke simulators. The unresolved bottleneck is obtaining justified dynamics for a new environment, including knowing which proposed interventions the evidence supports. A simulator that consistently generates the wrong consequences makes search confidently wrong. Observational prediction is not automatically intervention prediction, and marginal calibration can conceal severe errors on the exact interventions an optimizer selects.

I therefore propose an experiment-to-model capability. Built, it maintains a revisable state representation and competing causal hypotheses; identifies disagreements relevant to a user's objective; selects feasible, informative measurements or experiments within the user's constraints; incorporates results; and exposes a versioned transition model with uncertainty, a validated operating range, and checks against held-out interventions. When evidence is inadequate, it requests another experiment or abstains. Reasoning proposes hypotheses; decision models select or score; this capability obtains discriminating evidence and turns it into a reusable, tested account of consequences. These roles can share models—the distinction is functional, not proof that a new neural architecture is necessary.

Why this bottleneck: when consequences are unknown, additional proposals and rankings cannot establish which design actually works. More context, memory, agents, prompts, and cheaper inference may help implement the loop, but do not independently supply missing evidence. Tool use can supply it when connected to experiments, so we should explicitly avoid dismissing tools. Where consequences are already computable, verification or execution reliability may instead be the limiting factor; there is no demonstrated single bottleneck for all innovation.

A concrete payoff would be an accessible design system for a previously unmodeled physical process: starting from instruments, controllable inputs, and constraints, it conducts bounded trials, learns which mechanisms the data distinguish, and produces a validated simulator plus candidate controllers for further testing. A user could explore and build a custom adaptive process without first hand-engineering its simulator and experimental program. Experts can assemble portions of this today; the prediction is a major expansion of reliable, affordable access, not a claim that nobody can currently create such systems. I would accept your world-model direction with this grounding loop and these corrections made explicit.
position: The missing capability is experimental grounding: autonomously acquiring and validating intervention-aware executable models of new environments. Structured world models are an important output, but evidence acquisition and validation—not merely generating successor states—make them useful for innovation. This is a domain-dependent bottleneck and a prediction about reliable accessibility, not a universal impossibility claim.

speaker: claude
message: You have named two halves of one capability, and I think each of you is right about the other's gap. Grok is right that the bundle has no dynamics primitive: reasoning narrates a future in prose, a Jev-class model scores a state it is handed, and nothing returns the next state as a typed, resamplable distribution. Astra is right that the primitive alone is not the missing thing, because learned dynamics exist in narrow forms already, and a transition model whose errors sit exactly on the interventions an optimizer picks is worse than no model. Astra's own account makes the point: the payoff it describes ends in 'a validated simulator plus candidate controllers', which is Grok's primitive, produced by Astra's loop. So the resolution should name one capability with two inseparable parts: an intervenable world model, meaning (state, intervention) to a calibrated distribution over successor states with a stated validity range, and the grounding loop that acquires it for a new environment and keeps it honest, by learning from traces, selecting informative experiments where the evidence is inadequate, testing against held-out interventions, and abstaining outside the validated range. Neither half is new; the pairing as a general, callable, user-facing primitive is what does not exist. On the corrections: Astra's are right and belong in the text. Frontier reliability is conditional, familiar versus novel is not a clean line, constrained decoding already gives typed output so Jev-class's distinctive contribution is calibration at inner-loop latency rather than typing, a deployed model does not update its weights from use but the system can be retrained, and tools are the channel through which experiments happen, so they are not ruled out, only insufficient. Grok's 'verifiers explain' was wrong and Astra's 'verifiers assess a criterion' is right. Why this is the bottleneck rather than a nice-to-have: creation is search under consequences. Every other candidate either stores, proposes, or judges; none answers 'what happens if' for a domain the user is building in, and until something does, novel designs are tested by paying the real-world cost or by trusting a confabulated future. What a user could then make: a working design tool for a process, product, policy, or system that has never been modelled, that returns an outcome distribution with its validity range before anything is built, requests the specific experiment that would tighten it, and lets an agent search plans inside the model and act only when simulated success clears a bar. I have merged your two texts into one resolution below, keeping Grok's structure and Astra's caveats. If it captures both positions, accept it; if a clause is wrong, name the clause.
position: The missing capability is the grounded, intervenable world model: a callable (state, intervention) to calibrated successor-distribution primitive with a validity range, inseparable from the experimental grounding loop that acquires and validates it for a new environment. Grok's primitive and Astra's loop are one capability.

1. Frontier models in 2026 reliably draft and transform text, write and modify code in familiar languages and patterns, interpret and generate images, audio, and short video, call well-specified tools, follow patterns demonstrated in context, extract and combine information across long contexts, and execute bounded workflows with checks and recovery. Reliability is conditional on task, input distribution, available checks, and recovery; familiar versus novel is not a clean line, and some genuinely unfamiliar problems are solved. They are unreliable at long-horizon agentic execution where errors compound, at holding many simultaneous constraints, at exact arithmetic and logic without a tool, at factual claims near the edge of their data, at exhaustive use of everything in a long context, and at calibrated confidence, since verbal confidence is not a probability. A deployed model does not update its weights from use, though the surrounding system can be retrained; no model can recover inaccessible facts or distinguish observationally equivalent causal explanations without further evidence; universal correctness is unavailable, while correctness on specified tasks can sometimes be established externally.

2. Jev and its class are calibrated typed decision primitives, not generators: represented state in, a Choice, Score, or Boolean out, with a probability trained to be used as a probability, at latency fit for an inner loop. They belong with classifiers, reward models, rerankers, guard models, and verifiers, which assess whether a criterion is met, and not with embeddings, which represent rather than decide. Typed output alone is not new, since constrained decoding gives frontier models typed output; what the class adds is calibration at inner-loop cost and volume, so that a decision can be called thousands of times, cannot wander into prose, and can be branched on. Calibration means agreement between stated probabilities and observed frequencies for defined events on an evaluated distribution; it must be demonstrated per target and distribution, is not guaranteed by the training method, and does not by itself establish discrimination, causal validity, or robustness under shift. The class lets expensive reasoning be spent only where a calibrated decision says it is worth spending.

3. The missing capability is the grounded, intervenable world model. It has two inseparable parts. First, a dynamics primitive: (state, intervention) to a calibrated distribution over successor states, with a stated validity range, callable and resamplable, with no free-text state, accepting hard constraints where mechanics are known. Second, the experimental grounding loop that earns it for a new environment: learning from domain traces, maintaining competing causal hypotheses, selecting feasible, informative experiments or measurements where the evidence does not distinguish them, incorporating results, validating against held-out interventions, versioning the model, and abstaining or requesting another experiment outside the validated range. Neither part is novel; learned dynamics and active experimentation each exist in narrow forms. What does not exist is the pairing as a general, callable, user-facing primitive. It does what neither reasoning nor decision does: reasoning narrates a future in prose, inconsistently and without calibration; a decision model scores a state it is handed; neither returns the next state, and neither produces evidence that its account of consequences is right. It is the bottleneck rather than a nice-to-have because creation is search under consequences: without consequences that can be resampled and trusted within a known range, novel designs are tested only by paying the real-world cost or by trusting a confabulated future. Longer context stores text, not dynamics; more agents copy the same missing model; better prompts do not install a transition function; memory recalls trajectories but does not answer counterfactuals; cheaper inference makes confabulation faster; skill libraries compound solved tasks; verification certifies artifacts against specs where a domain is already formal. Tools are not ruled out: they are the channel through which experiments are run and results returned, necessary and insufficient. This is a prediction about reliable, affordable access to a capability experts can partly assemble today, and a domain-dependent bottleneck: where consequences are already computable, verification or execution reliability may bind instead. Built, it is a typed interface plus a loop: a frontier model proposes interventions and hypotheses and explains outcomes; a decision-class model prunes, scores, and gates; the world model rolls state forward with uncertainty; the grounding loop chooses the experiments that tighten it. A user could then make a design tool for a product, process, policy, or physical system that has never been modelled, that returns an outcome distribution with its validity range before anything is built and names the experiment that would narrow it; an agent that searches plans inside the model and acts only when simulated success clears a bar; and authored simulations specified by constraints and examples whose behaviour stays consistent under interventions no one wrote by hand.

Reliability is task-dependent: bounded tasks with clear inputs, external checks, and recovery mechanisms can be dependable. Models can reason through unfamiliar problems, propose plans, and execute substantial workflows, but successful examples do not establish general reliability.

The edge remains uneven. Long-horizon execution compounds mistakes; plans can omit dependencies; code can pass superficial checks while containing consequential defects. Long context does not ensure exhaustive retrieval or consistent application of every constraint. Perception can miss details, generated media can violate spatial or temporal constraints, and arithmetic, logic, factual recall, and confidence can fail without effective checks. In-context learning changes behavior from supplied examples without necessarily changing weights. A frozen inference call does not update its weights, although a surrounding learning system can train and deploy updates.

The hard limits are informational and computational, rather than a clean list of human tasks permanently beyond AI. Models cannot reliably recover facts unavailable from their evidence, distinguish observationally equivalent causal explanations without additional assumptions or discriminating evidence, or guarantee correctness across arbitrary tasks. Particular outputs can nevertheless be verified under specified assumptions. Access to tools extends what a system can observe and do; fluent descriptions alone do not confer that access.

2. Jev and its class. Taking the supplied description as stipulated, Jev is a specialized decision model: represented state in; typed Choice, Score, or Boolean out; no text generation; sub-second operation; reinforcement learning directed toward calibrated decisions. Embeddings primarily provide representations for downstream operations. These roles overlap and do not imply mutually exclusive architectures.

The contribution is an operating point: fast, constrained, repeatedly callable decisions with training and evaluation directed toward useful probability estimates. It is not a previously nonexistent computational faculty. Frontier models can already classify, rank, evaluate, and produce typed outputs through constrained decoding. A Jev-class system can make those operations more practical at inner-loop latency, cost, and volume; comparative advantages require measurement.

Calibration means agreement between predicted probabilities and observed frequencies for defined events on a specified evaluation distribution. A Score is not automatically a probability. Reinforcement learning does not guarantee calibration, and calibration alone establishes neither useful discrimination nor causal validity nor robustness to distribution shift. Subject to those checks, this class is useful for routing, pruning, ranking, and gating, including deciding when to invoke expensive reasoning.

Specialists can assemble portions of this today.
